reference_zone: Villa Mercedes / Central-East and Cuenca del Morro, San Luis, Argentina

methods.name: Productive Double Crop (Winter Wheat -> Double-Crop Soybean / Late Corn)
methods.sequence: Wheat (Autumn-Winter) -> Double-crop Soybean or Late Corn (Summer)
methods.horizon_label: Short term (1 year / intensive annual cycle)
methods.field_summary: Aims for two commercial grain harvests in a single year while keeping soil covered during strong August-September winds, but demands heavy water availability and tight planting windows.
methods.when_to_rotate: Apply only if initial soil moisture data and summer rainfall outlook are favorable (or under irrigation / non-saline shallow water table). Rotate immediately after winter wheat harvest.
methods.termination_criterion: Harvest wheat early (including artificial grain drying if needed) to avoid delaying second-crop planting; every week lost in December penalizes summer yield due to early autumn frosts.

criteria.name: Temperature patterns
criteria.justification: In Villa Mercedes, agrometeorological frosts (<3 C) span roughly from March to November. Waiting for wheat harvest delays second-crop planting, exposing grain fill to early autumn frosts (starting in April).

criteria.name: Heat stress
criteria.justification: Summers average 30-33 C highs. Wheat suffers spring heat waves during grain filling, and under rainfed conditions the second crop combines summer heat with water deficit.

criteria.name: Frost risk
criteria.justification: Highest cumulative exposure in Villa Mercedes: late frosts (Oct-Nov) during wheat heading and early autumn frosts during double-crop soybean/corn grain filling.

criteria.name: Extreme weather risks
criteria.justification: Exposes two commercial harvests to peak hailstorms, strong winds (wheat lodging/shattering and second-crop corn stalk breakage), and summer waterlogging.

criteria.name: Rainfall
criteria.justification: San Luis's dry winter (75-80% of rainfall occurs Oct-Mar) restricts rainfed wheat and leaves the profile depleted before second-crop planting. Only viable with irrigation or very wet eastern years (650-700 mm).

criteria.name: Soil moisture
criteria.justification: On sandy loam soils, wheat consumes autumn stored soil water and delivers a dry profile in Nov-Dec. Favorable only with supplemental irrigation or a non-saline shallow water table (1.5-3 m).

criteria.name: Evaporation (Evapotranspiration)
criteria.justification: Wheat stubble curbs direct summer soil evaporation, but the cumulative evapotranspiration demand of two harvested crops exceeds rainfed precipitation supply.

criteria.name: Long-term hydrological trends
criteria.justification: Under two annual harvests, deep soil reserves cannot recharge. During dry cycles (La Nina), risk of total crop failure rises sharply.

criteria.name: Water use efficiency
criteria.justification: High water demand in a semi-arid province; unless rainfall aligns precisely with both critical stages, both crops suffer yield loss.

criteria.name: Vegetation stress
criteria.justification: Under rainfed farming, subjects wheat to winter deficit and the second crop to water and oxidative stress over an already depleted profile.

criteria.name: Forage value
criteria.justification: Oriented almost exclusively toward grain sales; only late corn offers emergency silage without steady forage output.

criteria.name: Nitrogen fixation potential
criteria.justification: Negative balance: wheat and corn extract heavy N, and double-crop soybean exports more N in harvested grain than it fixes, creating strong fertilizer dependence.

criteria.name: Organic matter improvement
criteria.justification: Soybean residue degrades quickly and double annual nutrient extraction progressively wears down sandy soil structure.

criteria.name: Pests and diseases
criteria.justification: Without a winter biological break ('green bridge'), cutworms and pillbugs persist; aphids surge in dry wheat and fall armyworm (Spodoptera) plus leafhopper (Dalbulus maidis) peak in second-crop corn.

criteria.name: Market suitability
criteria.justification: Wheat, soybean, and corn enjoy daily public pricing (Matba Rofex), guaranteed export demand, and consolidated elevator logistics in Villa Mercedes toward ports.

sources.institution: INTA / CIAg - Pena Zubiate et al.
sources.title: Physical and Environmental Resources of San Luis Territories
sources.contribution: Villa Mercedes frost regime (03/29 +/- 24d to 11/09 +/- 19d) and summer rainfall share (75-80% Oct-Mar).

sources.title: Buenos Aires Futures Market
sources.contribution: Public price discovery, high liquidity, and hedging for wheat, soybean, and corn.

sources.title: Nitrogen Balance in Soybean-Wheat Rotations
sources.contribution: Documents net N export in harvested double-crop soybean grain.

methods.name: Anti-Water-Table & Anti-Erosion Biological Pump (Perennial Alfalfa -> Late Corn)
methods.horizon_label: Long term (4-5 years: perennial pasture + corn)
methods.field_summary: Keeps the field green for 3-4 years with deep roots that halt erosion, draw down excess water or rising water tables (such as Cuenca del Morro), and leave natural nitrogen for late corn.
methods.when_to_rotate: Establish alfalfa in autumn when the field needs nitrogen recovery, soil structure repair, or water-table drawdown. Rotate to late corn as alfalfa stand density declines (years 3-4).
methods.termination_criterion: Cut alfalfa at 10% bloom. Terminate pasture early in late winter (spring fallow) to recharge soil profile moisture before planting late corn in December (silking in February).

criteria.name: Temperature patterns
criteria.justification: Established alfalfa tolerates San Luis winter frosts; single-crop late corn can be planted in the optimal summer window.

criteria.name: Heat stress
criteria.justification: Deep taproots sustain summer transpiration; planting corn in December places silking in February, avoiding January heat waves.

criteria.name: Frost risk
criteria.justification: Autumn-established alfalfa resists winter frosts; December-planted corn avoids late November frosts and matures before April.

criteria.name: Extreme weather risks
criteria.justification: Alfalfa regrows from the crown after hail (losing only one cut) and does not lodge in high winds. Monitor root anoxia if ponding exceeds 48-72 h.

criteria.name: Rainfall
criteria.justification: Uses 600-800 mm/year capturing spring-summer rains and excess moisture. Requires timely pasture termination to recharge the profile before corn.

criteria.name: Soil moisture
criteria.justification: Outstanding performance where water tables are rising (Cuenca del Morro): lowers groundwater and prevents waterlogging. Leaves profile dry at exit, requiring spring fallow.

criteria.name: Evaporation (Evapotranspiration)
criteria.justification: Permanent canopy minimizes bare-soil evaporation and maximizes year-round transpiration to control rising groundwater.

criteria.name: Long-term hydrological trends
criteria.justification: Strong stabilizer against groundwater imbalances, restoring hydrological balance for subsequent cash cropping.

criteria.name: Water use efficiency
criteria.justification: Acts as a biological pump against groundwater excess and improves rainfall infiltration while curbing runoff.

criteria.name: Vegetation stress
criteria.justification: Deep taproot sustains photosynthesis during dry spells; late corn following fallow establishes canopy under milder summer conditions.

criteria.name: Forage value
criteria.justification: Unmatched option for beef/dairy livestock and high-protein hay production over 3-4 consecutive years.

criteria.name: Nitrogen fixation potential
criteria.justification: Biological atmospheric N factory for 3-4 years, supplying most of the nitrogen demand for subsequent late corn.

criteria.name: Organic matter improvement
criteria.justification: Zero tillage for 3-4 years; deep root biomass stabilizes soil aggregates and builds deep soil organic carbon.

criteria.name: Pests and diseases
criteria.justification: Breaks annual pest cycles and harbors beneficial insects. Watchpoints: aphids and alfalfa caterpillar (Colias lesbia), plus white grubs/cutworms/armyworm entering corn.

criteria.name: Market suitability
criteria.justification: Late corn has secure liquidity and alfalfa serves steady local feedlots/dairies plus compacted hay bale exports via AgroZAL in Villa Mercedes.

methods.name: Water Resilience / Defensive Strategy (Sorghum -> Vetch + Rye -> Sunflower)
methods.sequence: Sorghum (Summer 1) -> Vetch + Rye (Winter cover crop) -> Sunflower (Summer 2)
methods.horizon_label: Medium term (2 years: summer - winter bridge - summer)
methods.field_summary: Ideal defensive strategy for sandy soils and dry or erratic years: saves every millimeter of water with protective residue, adds free nitrogen via vetch, and diversifies low-water-demand crops.
methods.when_to_rotate: Adopt this scheme when soil moisture at planting is low or seasonal forecast is dry. Plant sorghum once spring soil warms; sow vetch + rye in autumn right after sorghum harvest.
methods.termination_criterion: Harvest sorghum grain or chop under severe stress. Terminate/roller-crimp vetch + rye in Sep/Oct (30-45 days before sunflower planting) to stop spring water extraction.

criteria.name: Temperature patterns
criteria.justification: Vetch + rye tolerate winter cold well as cover crops. Sorghum needs warm soils for germination, and sunflower requires timely planting before mid-November.

criteria.name: Heat stress
criteria.justification: Sorghum handles high heat better than corn, sunflower tolerates hot summers, and rye/vetch residue buffers soil surface temperature spikes.

criteria.name: Frost risk
criteria.justification: Winter cover suffers no grain loss; sorghum is frost-sensitive and heavy mulch can increase radiative frost risk for overly early sunflower plantings.

criteria.name: Extreme weather risks
criteria.justification: Stubble blocks spring wind erosion; sorghum tolerates brief waterlogging, while flowering sunflower remains vulnerable to hail and wind lodging.

criteria.name: Rainfall
criteria.justification: Best match for semi-arid rainfall (450-600 mm): sorghum and sunflower need less water than corn/soybean. Early Sep/Oct cover termination saves spring rain.

criteria.name: Soil moisture
criteria.justification: Most efficient approach on sandy soils without a shallow water table: curbs evaporation, boosts infiltration, and accesses subsoil moisture without depleting the profile when terminated on time.

criteria.name: Evaporation (Evapotranspiration)
criteria.justification: Persistent rye stubble (high C/N ratio) sharply cuts bare-soil evaporation while sorghum throttles transpiration under high atmospheric demand.

criteria.name: Long-term hydrological trends
criteria.justification: Progressive 'sponge' effect: accumulated ground cover enhances infiltration and soil water retention across future droughts.

criteria.name: Water use efficiency
criteria.justification: Ideal water-conservation design pairing sorghum's physiological drought resilience with a physical residue barrier.

criteria.name: Vegetation stress
criteria.justification: High plasticity: sorghum pauses growth during drought and recovers after rain; sunflower sustains photosynthesis via deep taproots.

criteria.name: Forage value
criteria.justification: Dual-purpose sorghum (grain or silage/deferred grazing) plus optional emergency grazing on vetch + rye while keeping basal residue cover.

criteria.name: Nitrogen fixation potential
criteria.justification: Vetch fixes atmospheric N and, since it is not harvested, 100% remains in the field for sunflower, lowering synthetic fertilizer needs.

criteria.name: Organic matter improvement
criteria.justification: Abundant, slowly decomposing sorghum and rye residue increases organic carbon and shields sandy soil structure.

criteria.name: Pests and diseases
criteria.justification: Maximum functional diversity (C4 grass -> C3 grass + legume mix -> broadleaf oilseed) breaks pest cycles. Monitor cutworms (Agrotis spp.) and pillbugs after vetch termination.

criteria.name: Market suitability
criteria.justification: More cyclical market (crushing quotas for sunflower or local/poultry-swine demand for sorghum), and winter cover carries an operational cost without direct cash harvest.
